explanation: The cable must match the port on each end: USB-C on the laptop and Micro-USB on the scanner. Such cables exist and carry USB 2.0 data and power, which is all a Micro-USB device can use. A Lightning cable is for Apple devices, a USB-A to USB-C cable has no Micro-USB end, and a Micro to Mini cable connects two legacy devices with nothing to plug into the laptop. Reading the connector on both ends is the whole task.

distractor_analysis.2: Lightning does not fit a Micro-USB port.
distractor_analysis.3: The laptop has no USB-A ports, and the scanner is not USB-C.
distractor_analysis.0: Neither end of that cable fits the laptop.

question: A user connects a USB-C phone to a USB-C monitor expecting the phone's screen to appear, but nothing displays. Charging works. What is the most likely reason?
options: USB-C can never carry video
The phone battery is too low to output video
The phone or the cable does not support DisplayPort Alternate Mode over USB-C
The monitor needs a Lightning input for phones
explanation: USB-C is a connector, not a guarantee of features. Video over USB-C requires DisplayPort Alternate Mode to be supported by the device, and the cable must be a full-featured one rather than a charge-only cable. Many phones charge over USB-C but do not implement Alt Mode at all, and some cheap cables carry only power and USB 2.0 data. Checking the phone's specification and using a cable rated for video resolves the confusion.

distractor_analysis.3: Lightning is an input on nothing; monitors do not have Lightning ports.
distractor_analysis.0: USB-C can carry DisplayPort and HDMI via alternate modes when supported.
distractor_analysis.1: Battery level does not disable video output.

question: A field technician wants to transfer photos from a phone to a laptop as fast as possible. The phone supports USB 3.2 over USB-C. Which cable choice matters most?
options: A cable that is at least three metres long
A cable with a braided jacket
A cable with a right-angle plug
A cable rated for USB 3.x data rather than a charge-only or USB 2.0 cable
explanation: USB-C cables vary widely in what they carry. Charge-only cables have no data wires, and many bundled cables carry only USB 2.0 at 480 Mbps. To reach USB 3.x speeds of 5 to 20 Gbps the cable itself must include the SuperSpeed wire pairs, which is usually marked on the packaging or the plug. Length, jacket and plug shape are convenience features that do not change the data rate, and very long cables can actually reduce reliable speed.

distractor_analysis.0: Longer cables lower signal integrity; length is not a speed feature.
distractor_analysis.1: Braiding improves durability, not bandwidth.
distractor_analysis.2: Plug angle is ergonomics only.

question: A user places a phone on a charging pad and it charges without any cable. Which standard is most commonly used for this?
options: USB Power Delivery
Qi wireless charging
Bluetooth
Near-field communication
explanation: Qi is the industry standard for inductive wireless charging in phones and earbuds. A coil in the pad induces current in a coil inside the phone when the two are aligned within a few millimetres. Charging is slower than a cable and generates more heat, and a thick metal case or a misaligned phone stops it working, which are the usual support questions. Bluetooth and NFC are data radios, and USB Power Delivery is a wired charging negotiation.

distractor_analysis.2: Bluetooth carries data and audio, not power.
distractor_analysis.3: NFC is used for taps and payments; the power it transfers is negligible.
distractor_analysis.0: Power Delivery works only over a USB-C cable.

question: A phone will not charge on a Qi pad but charges normally from a cable. The user recently added a thick case with a metal plate for a car mount. What should the technician recommend?
options: Switch the pad to a faster power adapter
Enable Bluetooth so the pad can pair with the phone
Remove the metal plate or case, because metal between the coils blocks inductive charging
Replace the phone's charging port
explanation: Inductive charging relies on a magnetic field coupling the pad's coil to the phone's coil. A metal plate in the path absorbs the field, heats up and prevents the phone charging, and even a thick non-metal case can push the coils too far apart. Cable charging works because it bypasses the coil entirely, which rules out a port fault. Adapter wattage and Bluetooth have no role in whether the inductive link forms.

distractor_analysis.3: The port is proven working by the successful cable charge.
distractor_analysis.0: A stronger adapter cannot push a field through metal.
distractor_analysis.1: Qi pads do not pair over Bluetooth.

question: A user wants to pay for coffee by holding a phone near the card terminal. Which short-range technology makes this possible?
options: Bluetooth Low Energy
Infrared
Wi-Fi Direct
Near-field communication
explanation: NFC operates over a few centimetres at 13.56 MHz and is what contactless payment systems such as Apple Pay and Google Wallet use to exchange a tokenised card credential with the terminal. The very short range is a security feature. NFC is also used to pair Bluetooth accessories with a tap and to read tags. Bluetooth reaches metres and needs pairing, infrared was an old line-of-sight link for early PDAs, and Wi-Fi Direct is for file transfer between devices.

distractor_analysis.0: Bluetooth's range and pairing model are unsuitable for tap-to-pay.
distractor_analysis.1: Infrared beaming is obsolete and needs line of sight.
distractor_analysis.2: Wi-Fi Direct is peer-to-peer file transfer, not payment.

question: A user's contactless payments stopped working after they put the phone in a new wallet case with several cards inside. Payments work when the phone is taken out of the case. What is the cause?
options: The payment app needs to be reinstalled
The other contactless cards in the case interfere with the phone's NFC field
The case has disabled the phone's Bluetooth radio
The phone's battery is too low for NFC
explanation: NFC terminals read one credential at a time. When a wallet case places bank cards directly over the phone's NFC antenna, the terminal sees multiple contactless targets and either rejects the read or the cards absorb the field so the phone cannot respond. Removing the cards, or using a case with a shielding layer, fixes it. The successful payments outside the case prove the radio, battery and app are all fine.

distractor_analysis.2: Contactless payment uses NFC, and a case cannot switch off a radio.
distractor_analysis.3: Payments work outside the case at the same battery level.
distractor_analysis.0: The app works as soon as the phone leaves the case.

question: Which wireless technology is used to connect a phone to a car's hands-free system and to wireless earbuds?
options: Cellular
GPS
Bluetooth
NFC
explanation: Bluetooth is the short-range personal area network radio used for audio accessories, keyboards, wearables and car hands-free systems. Devices are paired once, after which they reconnect automatically when in range of roughly ten metres. Modern devices use Bluetooth Low Energy for wearables and sensors and classic Bluetooth profiles for audio. NFC only reaches a few centimetres, cellular is the wide-area voice and data network, and GPS is receive-only positioning.

distractor_analysis.3: NFC is sometimes used to trigger the pairing, but the audio link is Bluetooth.
distractor_analysis.0: Cellular connects to the carrier network, not to local accessories.
distractor_analysis.1: GPS receives satellite signals and cannot connect to accessories.

question: Wireless earbuds that paired to a phone yesterday will not connect today. They appear in the paired list but show as disconnected. The earbuds are charged. What should the user try first?
options: Factory reset the phone
Replace the earbuds
Enable Airplane mode permanently
Turn Bluetooth off and on, or forget the earbuds and pair them again
explanation: Stale pairing state is the most common Bluetooth complaint. Toggling the radio forces a reconnection attempt, and if that fails, removing the device from the paired list and pairing fresh rebuilds the link keys on both ends. Also check the earbuds are not still connected to another device such as a laptop, because most earbuds hold one active connection. A phone reset or new hardware is disproportionate, and Airplane mode disables the radio you need.

distractor_analysis.0: A full reset destroys user data to fix a pairing key.
distractor_analysis.1: The hardware is not shown to be faulty.
distractor_analysis.2: Airplane mode turns Bluetooth off by default.

question: A user wants to pair a new Bluetooth keyboard but the phone never lists it. The keyboard's light is on. What is the most likely reason?
options: The phone's Wi-Fi is turned off
The keyboard is not in pairing mode, so it is not advertising itself
The phone needs an NFC tag to discover keyboards
Bluetooth keyboards only work with laptops
explanation: A Bluetooth accessory only becomes discoverable when it is put into pairing mode, usually by holding a dedicated button until an LED blinks in a distinctive pattern. A power light alone means it is on, possibly still bound to a previous device. Once in pairing mode it appears in the phone's list within seconds and a PIN or confirmation completes the process. NFC is optional, keyboards work with any Bluetooth host, and Wi-Fi is a separate radio.

distractor_analysis.2: NFC tap-to-pair is a convenience on some accessories, never a requirement.
distractor_analysis.3: Phones and tablets support Bluetooth HID keyboards.
distractor_analysis.0: Bluetooth discovery does not depend on Wi-Fi.

question: A photographer wants to move a stack of raw images from a phone to a laptop in a location with no Wi-Fi and no cable. Both devices support Bluetooth. Why might the technician still advise against Bluetooth for this task?
options: Bluetooth requires an internet connection
Bluetooth transfers are not encrypted
Bluetooth's data rate is low, so a large transfer takes a very long time
Bluetooth cannot transfer image files
explanation: Bluetooth is designed for low power and modest bandwidth. Even Bluetooth 5 tops out at around 2 Mbps in practice, so several gigabytes of raw photos would take hours. Wi-Fi Direct, a phone hotspot or a USB cable are all far faster. Bluetooth can transfer any file type, needs no internet and does encrypt its links; its only real limitation for this job is speed, which is why it is used for audio and small data rather than bulk transfer.

distractor_analysis.3: Bluetooth file transfer supports any file type.
distractor_analysis.0: Bluetooth is a direct device-to-device link with no internet dependency.
distractor_analysis.1: Bluetooth links are encrypted after pairing.

question: A laptop with a single USB-C port needs to connect to a wired network, an HDMI projector, a USB-A mouse and a charger at the same time. Which accessory meets the requirement?
options: A USB-A to Ethernet adapter
A Lightning to HDMI adapter
A Qi charging pad
A USB-C docking station or multiport hub with Power Delivery pass-through
explanation: A docking station or multiport hub expands one USB-C connection into several interfaces: Ethernet, HDMI or DisplayPort, USB-A ports and a USB-C power input that passes charging through to the laptop. This is the standard accessory for thin laptops with few ports. A single-purpose USB-A Ethernet adapter does not fit a USB-C port and covers only one need, Lightning belongs to older Apple phones, and a Qi pad charges phones, not laptops.

distractor_analysis.0: It has the wrong plug for the laptop and solves only the network need.
distractor_analysis.1: Lightning is not a laptop connector.
distractor_analysis.2: Qi is inductive phone charging and provides no ports.

question: A user reports that the laptop does not charge while connected to a new USB-C hub, although the monitor and keyboard attached to the hub work. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The monitor cable is too long
The hub lacks a Power Delivery pass-through port or the charger is plugged into the laptop's port on the hub rather than the hub's power input
USB-C hubs are not capable of charging laptops
The keyboard is drawing all the available power
explanation: Many inexpensive hubs have a data-only USB-C port and no power input, so the laptop must be charged separately. Hubs that do support charging have a clearly marked PD input port; plugging the charger into an ordinary downstream port does nothing for the laptop. Checking the hub's specification for a PD pass-through rating at or above the laptop's wattage is the fix. Hubs certainly can charge laptops when built for it, a keyboard draws a few milliamps, and cable length does not affect charging.

distractor_analysis.2: Docking stations charge laptops routinely through PD pass-through.
distractor_analysis.3: A keyboard's draw is negligible.
distractor_analysis.0: Video cable length has no bearing on the power path.

question: Which accessory is designed to hold a tablet steady while an artist draws on it with a stylus?
options: A screen protector
A USB-C hub
An adjustable stand or drawing tripod
A wireless charging pad
explanation: Stands and mounts are simple accessories that matter a great deal to usability: an adjustable stand tilts a tablet to a comfortable drawing angle and keeps it stable under stylus pressure. Technicians are often asked to recommend mounts for point-of-sale tablets, kiosks and vehicles as well. A charging pad supplies power, a screen protector guards the glass and a hub adds ports; none of them positions the device.

distractor_analysis.3: Charging pads power the device but do not hold it at an angle.
distractor_analysis.0: Screen protectors protect the glass but provide no support.
distractor_analysis.1: Hubs add connectivity, not positioning.

question: A user applied a tempered glass screen protector and now the phone's fingerprint sensor under the display fails most of the time. What is the correct advice?
options: The sensor is broken and the phone needs repair
Disable the screen protector in settings
Fingerprint sensors never work with any protector
Use a protector certified for in-display fingerprint sensors, then re-enrol the fingerprint through the protector
explanation: Optical and ultrasonic in-display sensors read the finger through the glass. A thick or air-gapped protector scatters the light or dampens the ultrasound and the stored template no longer matches. Protectors made for that phone model are thin and optically clear over the sensor area, and re-enrolling with the protector fitted gives the sensor a template that matches what it now sees. The hardware is fine, protectors are not software, and correctly chosen protectors work well.

distractor_analysis.0: The sensor worked before the protector; the glass is the variable.
distractor_analysis.1: A protector is a physical film; there is nothing to disable.
distractor_analysis.2: Compatible protectors are sold specifically for these sensors.

question: A delivery company needs to attach phones to delivery bikes in all weather and still charge them during the shift. Which combination of accessories fits the requirement?
options: A tempered glass protector and a USB hub
A rugged waterproof case with a handlebar mount and a weather-sealed charging solution
A leather wallet case and a desktop charging pad
A clear silicone case and a Bluetooth keyboard
explanation: The requirement is protection from impact and water, secure attachment to a vehicle, and power on the move. A rugged, ingress-rated case, a locking handlebar mount and a sealed charging path such as a covered USB port or a wireless charging mount meet all three. Wallet cases and desk pads suit an office, a keyboard is irrelevant on a bike, and a hub and protector solve neither mounting nor weather.

distractor_analysis.2: Leather and a desk pad do not survive rain or stay on a bike.
distractor_analysis.3: A keyboard is unusable on a moving vehicle.
distractor_analysis.0: Neither item mounts or protects the phone.

question: A user's phone battery does not last a full day of travel. Which accessory gives the simplest fix without any repair?
options: A screen protector
A car mount
A portable battery pack (power bank)
A Bluetooth headset
explanation: A power bank is a portable battery with USB outputs that recharges a phone anywhere. Technicians should advise on capacity in milliamp-hours relative to the phone's battery, on output wattage if fast charging is wanted, and on airline rules that limit lithium batteries in carry-on to roughly 100 Wh. The other accessories change how the phone is used or protected but do nothing for runtime.

distractor_analysis.3: A headset consumes power rather than supplying it.
distractor_analysis.0: A protector guards the glass only.
distractor_analysis.1: A mount holds the phone but does not charge it unless it is a charging mount.

question: A user's phone charges very slowly from a power bank that is rated 10,000 mAh with a 5 V 1 A output. The phone supports 25 W fast charging. Why is charging slow?
options: The power bank's capacity is too small to fast charge
The phone is set to low power mode
Power banks cannot fast charge any phone
The power bank's output is only 5 W, far below what the phone can accept
explanation: Charging speed is set by the output power, which is voltage times current. A 5 V 1 A output is 5 W regardless of the bank's capacity in milliamp-hours, which only describes how much energy is stored. To fast charge, the bank must support USB Power Delivery or the phone's proprietary protocol at 18 to 25 W or more. Capacity is unrelated to rate, low power mode does not throttle charging, and PD-capable power banks fast charge normally.

distractor_analysis.0: Capacity is how much energy is stored, not how fast it is delivered.
distractor_analysis.1: Low power mode reduces consumption; it does not slow charging.
distractor_analysis.2: Many power banks support PD fast charging at 20 W or more.

question: Which type of USB-C cable is required to connect a laptop to a 40 Gbps Thunderbolt 4 dock and use its full bandwidth?
options: A Lightning cable with a USB-C end
A Thunderbolt-certified cable, marked with the lightning-bolt symbol
Any USB-C charging cable
A USB 2.0 rated USB-C cable
explanation: Thunderbolt uses the USB-C connector but demands a cable built to its specification, identified by the lightning-bolt logo and, for longer runs, active electronics in the plug. A generic USB-C cable may negotiate only USB 3 or even USB 2 speeds, so the dock's displays and drives underperform or fail to appear. Charging-grade and USB 2.0 cables lack the high-speed pairs, and a Lightning cable is for older Apple phones.

distractor_analysis.2: Charging cables often omit high-speed data lines entirely.
distractor_analysis.3: USB 2.0 cables cap at 480 Mbps.
distractor_analysis.0: Lightning cables connect old iPhones and carry USB 2.0 only.

question: A user complains that a phone connected to a laptop over USB-C only offers charging, and the laptop cannot see the phone's files. Which step on the phone fixes this?
options: Turn on the mobile hotspot
Insert a memory card
Change the USB connection mode from charging only to file transfer
Enable Bluetooth
explanation: Phones default to charge-only when connected to a computer as a privacy protection. A notification appears offering USB options, and selecting file transfer (MTP) or photo transfer (PTP) exposes the storage to the computer. On some phones the device must also be unlocked and a trust prompt accepted. Bluetooth and hotspot are unrelated radios, and a memory card adds storage without changing the USB mode.

distractor_analysis.3: Bluetooth is a separate wireless link and does not change the USB mode.
distractor_analysis.0: Hotspot shares the phone's internet connection.
distractor_analysis.1: Storage is present; the phone is simply not exposing it.

question: A phone charges only when the cable is held at an angle, and lint is visible inside the port. What should the technician do first?
options: Replace the phone's battery
Push the cable in harder to compress the debris
Apply contact cleaner spray into the port while the phone is on
Power the phone off and carefully remove debris from the port with a non-conductive tool
explanation: Pocket lint packs into the bottom of charging ports and stops the plug seating fully, producing exactly this angle-dependent charging. With the phone off, a wooden or plastic pick lifts the debris out without shorting or scratching the contacts, and a quick check with a light confirms the port is clear. Only if a clean port still charges intermittently is the port or its flex cable suspect. Forcing the cable damages the port, and spraying liquid into a powered device risks a short.

distractor_analysis.0: The battery is not implicated by a mechanical seating problem.
distractor_analysis.1: Force bends the port's contacts and worsens the fault.
distractor_analysis.2: Liquids and a powered device are a short-circuit risk.

question: A user has a tablet with a proprietary magnetic connector on its edge. Which accessory is this connector most likely designed for?
options: A detachable keyboard cover that draws power and data from the tablet
A Qi wireless charging pad
A pair of Bluetooth earbuds
An NFC payment terminal
explanation: Tablet makers add a magnetic pogo-pin connector along one edge so a keyboard cover can attach without pairing or charging: the tablet supplies power and the keys send data over the pins. Because it is proprietary, only the vendor's or licensed keyboards fit. Wireless charging uses a coil behind the back glass, earbuds connect over Bluetooth, and payments use the NFC antenna; none of them use an edge connector.

distractor_analysis.1: Qi charging is coil-based and needs no physical connector.
distractor_analysis.2: Earbuds pair over Bluetooth.
distractor_analysis.3: NFC is contactless.

question: A user wants to use a stylus for handwritten notes on a tablet, but a cheap capacitive stylus gives thick imprecise lines. What should the technician recommend?
options: An active stylus supported by the tablet, which offers a fine tip, pressure sensitivity and palm rejection
A larger capacitive stylus
A screen protector to make the surface smoother
Increasing the display brightness
explanation: A passive capacitive stylus is simply a conductive rubber tip that imitates a fingertip, so the tablet sees a large blunt contact. An active stylus communicates with the digitizer, often over Bluetooth or a vendor protocol, to report a precise tip position, pressure and tilt, and lets the tablet ignore the resting palm. It must be a model the tablet supports. Bigger passive tips make lines coarser, and protectors and brightness do not change the input precision.

distractor_analysis.1: A larger passive tip is even less precise.
distractor_analysis.2: A protector changes feel, not digitizer resolution.
distractor_analysis.3: Brightness affects visibility only.

question: An office wants to connect an older Lightning iPhone to a conference room display with HDMI input for a presentation. Which accessory is needed?
options: A Lightning to HDMI digital adapter
A USB-C to HDMI cable
A Micro-USB to HDMI MHL adapter
A DisplayPort cable
explanation: Lightning iPhones output video through an Apple-certified Lightning digital AV adapter that provides an HDMI port and a Lightning pass-through for charging. Uncertified adapters frequently fail or stop working after updates. USB-C to HDMI suits newer iPhones and Android phones with Alt Mode, MHL was a Micro-USB era Android standard, and a DisplayPort cable has no end that fits the phone.

distractor_analysis.1: The phone has a Lightning port, not USB-C.
distractor_analysis.2: MHL adapters are for Micro-USB Android phones and are largely obsolete.
distractor_analysis.3: Neither end of a DisplayPort cable fits a phone.

question: A user complains that a Bluetooth headset connected to a phone has audio that lags noticeably behind video. Which factor is the most likely cause?
options: The audio codec and buffering used over Bluetooth introduce latency
The phone's Wi-Fi is turned off
The headset is in pairing mode
The phone has no SIM card
explanation: Bluetooth audio is compressed and buffered before transmission, which adds tens to hundreds of milliseconds of delay depending on the codec. Basic SBC has the most lag; codecs such as aptX Low Latency or AAC with a well-matched headset reduce it, and many video apps compensate automatically. The delay is inherent to the wireless link, not a fault. Wi-Fi, pairing state and cellular service have no bearing on the timing of audio already playing.

distractor_analysis.1: Wi-Fi is not involved in a local Bluetooth stream.
distractor_analysis.2: A headset in pairing mode would not be playing audio.
distractor_analysis.3: Cellular service has nothing to do with local audio playback.

question: A field technician wants a USB-C phone to read files from a USB-A flash drive. Which single accessory makes this possible?
options: A USB-C on-the-go adapter or hub that provides a USB-A host port
A Lightning to USB camera adapter
A Qi receiver coil
An NFC tag
explanation: Phones and tablets can act as a USB host, a capability called USB On-The-Go. A small USB-C to USB-A OTG adapter lets the phone power and mount a flash drive, and a hub does the same for several devices at once. Once attached, the files app shows the drive. The Lightning camera adapter does this job for older iPhones only, and a Qi coil or an NFC tag has nothing to do with USB storage.

distractor_analysis.1: The camera adapter has a Lightning plug and will not fit USB-C.
distractor_analysis.2: Qi receivers are for wireless charging.
distractor_analysis.3: NFC tags store a few hundred bytes and cannot host a drive.

question: A phone's NFC payment works, but tapping it against an NFC-equipped speaker does not start Bluetooth pairing as advertised. Which setting is most likely the cause?
options: NFC tag reading or the tap-to-pair feature is disabled on the phone, or the phone is an iPhone that does not support NFC pairing this way
The speaker needs Wi-Fi
The phone's SIM is locked
The speaker battery is too full
explanation: NFC pairing works by reading a tag in the accessory that carries the Bluetooth address and then completing the pairing automatically. Android phones must have NFC enabled and often have a separate toggle for reading tags; iPhones restrict background NFC use so this convenience does not work with most speakers. Payment working shows the NFC radio is fine, so the issue is the feature or platform, not the hardware. Wi-Fi, SIM state and battery level are irrelevant.

distractor_analysis.1: Bluetooth speakers do not need Wi-Fi.
distractor_analysis.2: SIM lock affects cellular service only.
distractor_analysis.3: A full battery does not disable pairing.

question: A user reports that a laptop connected through a USB-C dock loses its external monitors whenever a large file copies to a dock-attached SSD. What is the most likely cause?
options: The dock is sharing limited USB-C bandwidth between DisplayPort and USB data, and the link renegotiates under load
The monitors are too bright
The SSD is formatted with the wrong file system
The laptop's Bluetooth is interfering with the dock
explanation: A single USB-C link has a fixed number of high-speed lanes. When the dock is not Thunderbolt, DisplayPort video and USB 3 data must share those lanes, and heavy storage traffic can force a renegotiation that briefly drops the displays. Solutions include a Thunderbolt dock and cable, lowering monitor resolution or refresh rate, or moving the SSD to a port on the laptop itself. Brightness, file system and Bluetooth do not affect lane allocation.

distractor_analysis.1: Brightness is a monitor setting with no link impact.
distractor_analysis.2: File system affects compatibility, not the physical link.
distractor_analysis.3: Bluetooth is a separate radio and does not touch the USB-C link.

question: A user has connected a USB-C laptop charger to a phone. What happens?
options: The phone negotiates a safe power level with the charger and charges normally
The phone is damaged by the higher voltage
The phone will not charge because laptop chargers are incompatible
The charger switches off permanently
explanation: USB-C Power Delivery is a negotiation. The charger advertises the voltages and currents it can provide and the phone requests only the profile it can accept, typically 9 V at 2 to 3 A. A 65 W or 100 W laptop charger therefore charges a phone safely and often faster than the phone's own small adapter. This is the interoperability benefit of USB-C, and technicians can reassure users that PD-compliant chargers are safe across device classes.

distractor_analysis.1: PD starts at 5 V and only raises voltage on request, so no damage occurs.
distractor_analysis.2: PD-compliant chargers work across phones, tablets and laptops.
distractor_analysis.3: Chargers do not disable themselves when a smaller device is attached.

question: Which statement about hotspot capability is correct when a user wants a laptop to get online through a phone in a location with no Wi-Fi?
options: The phone can share its cellular connection over Wi-Fi, Bluetooth or USB tethering
Tethering requires a Lightning cable
Only tablets can create hotspots
Hotspots work only when the phone is on Wi-Fi
explanation: Phones can share their mobile data three ways. A Wi-Fi hotspot is the most common and supports several clients, USB tethering charges the phone while offering a stable wired link to one laptop, and Bluetooth tethering is low power but slow. The carrier plan must allow tethering. The phone's connector type is irrelevant to the feature, phones and tablets both offer it, and a hotspot specifically shares the cellular link rather than Wi-Fi.

distractor_analysis.1: USB tethering works over whatever USB cable the phone uses.
distractor_analysis.2: Phones are the most common hotspot devices.
distractor_analysis.3: A hotspot shares cellular data; it is not dependent on Wi-Fi.

question: A user wants a wireless keyboard and mouse for a tablet but does not want to pair or charge anything. Which option is not viable and why?
options: A 2.4 GHz keyboard with a USB receiver is impractical because the tablet may lack a USB-A port and the receiver still needs one
Bluetooth is not viable because tablets cannot use keyboards
A wired keyboard is not viable because tablets have no input capability
An NFC keyboard is the only working option
explanation: Proprietary 2.4 GHz peripherals avoid Bluetooth pairing but need their small USB receiver plugged in, which a tablet with only USB-C can accommodate only through an OTG adapter, and the receiver protrudes from the device. Bluetooth is the natural fit for tablets and pairs once. A wired keyboard also works through an adapter. There is no such thing as an NFC keyboard; NFC carries too little data for continuous input.

distractor_analysis.1: Tablets support Bluetooth keyboards natively.
distractor_analysis.2: Wired keyboards work through a USB-C OTG adapter.
distractor_analysis.3: NFC has no role in continuous keyboard input.

question: A phone's screen has fine scratches after months in a pocket with keys. The user asks how to prevent this on the replacement phone. What is the best advice?
options: Fit a tempered glass or film screen protector and a case as soon as the phone is unboxed
Increase the display brightness so scratches are less visible
Store the phone with the screen facing the keys so the back takes the damage
Apply furniture polish to the glass weekly
explanation: Screen protectors exist for exactly this reason: a sacrificial layer of tempered glass or film takes the scratches and can be replaced for a few pounds, while a case protects the edges and back from drops. Applying them before the first day of use avoids trapping dust or fitting over existing damage. Brightness does not remove scratches, deliberately facing the keys guarantees damage, and polish contains abrasives and oils that harm oleophobic coatings.

distractor_analysis.1: Brightness cannot hide physical scratches.
distractor_analysis.2: Facing the keys is the cause of the problem, not the solution.
distractor_analysis.3: Polishes can strip the coating and add micro-scratches.

question: A car's USB port charges a phone but the car's infotainment system does not recognise the phone for wired screen projection. The same phone and cable work in another car. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The car's port is a charge-only port; the data-capable port is elsewhere
The phone needs a new SIM card
The cable is too short
Screen projection requires NFC
explanation: Vehicles often have several USB ports, and only one or two are wired to the head unit for data; the rest are charging outlets with no data lines. Because the phone and cable are proven in another car, the variable is the port. Moving to the port marked with the data or projection symbol, or consulting the vehicle manual, resolves it. A SIM affects cellular service, cable length does not stop enumeration, and wired projection needs USB data rather than NFC.

distractor_analysis.1: Cellular service is not required for wired projection.
distractor_analysis.2: A short cable still carries data.
distractor_analysis.3: NFC is not part of wired screen projection.

question: A technician is asked which two features of USB-C make it different from the Micro-USB it replaced on phones. Which TWO are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: The plug is reversible and inserts either way up
It can negotiate much higher charging power through Power Delivery
It is limited to USB 2.0 speeds
It only works with Apple devices
It requires a separate power connector for charging
explanation: USB-C brought two everyday improvements: a symmetrical plug that cannot be inserted the wrong way, and the Power Delivery protocol that raises charging from the 7.5 W or so of Micro-USB to 100 W and beyond, enough for laptops. Depending on the device it can also carry USB 3.x or Thunderbolt data and DisplayPort video. It is an open standard used across every platform and carries power and data in the one connector.

distractor_analysis.2: USB-C can carry USB 3.x, USB4 and Thunderbolt; only the cheapest cables are limited to USB 2.0.
distractor_analysis.3: USB-C is an industry standard used by Android, Windows, Apple and others.
distractor_analysis.4: Power and data share the single connector.

question: A user's phone will not wirelessly charge on a Qi pad that works for a colleague's phone. Which TWO checks should the technician make first? (Select TWO.)
options: Confirm the phone model actually supports wireless charging
Remove the case and re-centre the phone on the pad
Update the phone's Bluetooth firmware
Insert a higher-capacity SIM card
Enable the phone's mobile hotspot
explanation: Two things account for almost every wireless charging complaint. Not every phone has a receiving coil, especially budget models, so the specification must be checked. When the phone does support it, a thick or metallic case or a phone lying off-centre breaks the coupling between coils, and simply removing the case and aligning the phone over the pad's marked area restores charging. Bluetooth, SIM and hotspot are unrelated to inductive charging.

distractor_analysis.2: Bluetooth has no role in wireless charging.
distractor_analysis.3: SIM cards carry subscriber identity and have no effect on charging.
distractor_analysis.4: Hotspot shares data and, if anything, drains the battery.

question: Match each mobile connection technology to its typical use.

pairs.right: Contactless payment within a few centimetres
Wireless earbuds and car hands-free within about ten metres
Fast wired charging and data for phones and laptops
Cable-free inductive charging on a pad
Proprietary connector on older Apple phones

explanation: Each technology has a distinct job. NFC is deliberately short range for secure taps. Bluetooth is the personal area network for accessories. USB-C with Power Delivery is the universal wired connection that negotiates charging power. Qi is the inductive charging standard. Lightning was Apple's proprietary plug before its move to USB-C. Knowing which one is in play tells the technician where to look when a connection fails.

question: Put the steps for pairing a new Bluetooth headset with a phone in the correct order.
sequence: Charge the headset and confirm the phone's Bluetooth is turned on
Hold the headset's pairing button until its light blinks in pairing mode
Open the phone's Bluetooth settings and select the headset from the list of available devices
Confirm any PIN or pairing prompt and wait for the status to show connected
Play audio to verify the headset is the active output
explanation: Pairing fails most often because a step is skipped: the headset is not actually in pairing mode, or the phone's radio is off. Putting the accessory into pairing mode makes it discoverable, the phone then lists it, and confirming the prompt exchanges the link keys that let the two reconnect automatically in future. Testing audio confirms the phone has actually routed sound to the new device rather than to its own speaker.

question: A company buys a mixed fleet of USB-C phones and laptops and wants one type of desk charger for every desk. Which specification should the technician require?
options: USB-C Power Delivery chargers rated at or above the highest laptop wattage in the fleet
Micro-USB chargers rated 10 W
Lightning chargers rated 20 W
Any USB-A charger with an adapter cable
explanation: Because Power Delivery negotiates downward, a single charger rated for the most demanding laptop, commonly 65 W or 100 W, will also charge every phone and tablet safely. Standardising on it simplifies procurement and support. Micro-USB and Lightning are the wrong connectors for a USB-C fleet, and USB-A chargers cannot supply the voltages laptops need, so an adapter cable would leave the laptops uncharged.

distractor_analysis.1: Micro-USB is the wrong connector and far too little power.
distractor_analysis.2: Lightning is Apple-specific and not a laptop connector.
distractor_analysis.3: USB-A ports top out around 12 to 18 W and cannot run laptops.

question: A user's phone shows 5G in the status bar at home but only LTE in a rural area. Both allow calls and browsing. What does the change indicate?
options: The phone has fallen back to the older cellular network generation available in that location
The phone's SIM card has been deactivated
The phone has switched to Wi-Fi calling
The phone's cellular radio has failed
explanation: Cellular phones hold radios for several generations and use the fastest one the nearest tower offers. 5G coverage is concentrated in cities, so a phone that shows 5G at home and LTE (4G) in the countryside is behaving correctly and will still make calls and pass data, just at lower peak speeds. A deactivated SIM would show no service, Wi-Fi calling shows its own indicator, and a failed radio would leave the phone with no cellular signal at all.

distractor_analysis.1: A deactivated SIM produces no service rather than a slower generation.
distractor_analysis.2: Wi-Fi calling has its own status indicator and needs a Wi-Fi network.
distractor_analysis.3: A failed radio shows no signal, not LTE.

question: A phone has a strong Wi-Fi signal but web pages will not load, while the same pages load fine on cellular data. What should the technician check first?
options: Whether the Wi-Fi network has internet access or requires a captive portal sign-in
Whether the phone's SIM card is seated
Whether Bluetooth is enabled
Whether the phone needs a new battery
explanation: Signal strength only shows that the phone is associated with the access point. A hotel, airport or guest network usually demands a captive-portal login before it forwards traffic, and a home router can lose its upstream connection while still broadcasting a strong Wi-Fi signal. Opening a browser to trigger the portal, or checking the router's internet light, resolves most cases. The SIM is proven fine by working cellular data, and Bluetooth and the battery are unrelated.

distractor_analysis.1: Cellular data works, so the SIM is seated and active.
distractor_analysis.2: Bluetooth has no role in Wi-Fi internet access.
distractor_analysis.3: Battery state does not block web traffic.

question: A traveller wants to stop a phone using any radio during a flight but still listen to downloaded music with wired headphones. Which setting achieves this?
options: Airplane mode
Do Not Disturb
Low power mode
Data roaming off
explanation: Airplane mode disables the cellular, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radios in one switch while leaving the rest of the phone usable, so offline music, downloaded films and local apps continue to work. On most phones Wi-Fi and Bluetooth can be re-enabled individually while airplane mode stays on, which is how in-flight Wi-Fi and wireless earbuds are used. Do Not Disturb only silences notifications, low power mode throttles performance, and data roaming controls only cellular data abroad.

distractor_analysis.1: Do Not Disturb leaves every radio on.
distractor_analysis.2: Low power mode saves battery but does not disable radios.
distractor_analysis.3: Data roaming is a cellular billing control, not a radio switch.

question: A user returns from abroad to a very large phone bill. The phone was used for maps and email throughout the trip. Which setting would have prevented the charges?
options: Turning off data roaming, or buying a travel data plan before departure
Turning off Bluetooth
Enabling Do Not Disturb
Lowering the screen brightness
explanation: Roaming means the phone attaches to a foreign carrier's network, and data used there is billed at that carrier's rates unless the home plan includes roaming. Disabling data roaming makes the phone use only Wi-Fi for data abroad, and a travel plan or local SIM caps the cost. Technicians supporting travelling staff should set expectations before the trip. Bluetooth, notification settings and brightness have no effect on cellular data charges.

distractor_analysis.1: Bluetooth uses no cellular data.
distractor_analysis.2: Do Not Disturb hides alerts but apps still sync in the background.
distractor_analysis.3: Brightness affects battery, not billing.

question: A user needs to work on a laptop in a park with no Wi-Fi. The phone has a good cellular signal. What is the quickest way to get the laptop online?
options: Enable the phone's Wi-Fi hotspot and join the laptop to it
Pair the laptop and phone over NFC
Plug the phone into the laptop's HDMI port
Enable airplane mode on the phone
explanation: A hotspot turns the phone into a small Wi-Fi access point that shares its cellular data connection. The laptop joins it like any other network, using the password shown on the phone. Technicians should remind users that hotspot use counts against the phone plan's data allowance, drains the battery quickly, and that USB tethering is an alternative that charges the phone at the same time. NFC and HDMI do not carry internet, and airplane mode would switch the cellular radio off.

distractor_analysis.1: NFC exchanges tiny amounts of data at very short range.
distractor_analysis.2: HDMI carries video, not network traffic.
distractor_analysis.3: Airplane mode disables the very radio that provides the data.

question: A phone's location in a mapping app is accurate outdoors but jumps around or is unavailable inside a large building. Why?
options: GPS needs a clear view of satellites, and indoors the phone falls back to less precise Wi-Fi and cellular positioning
The phone's SIM card cannot be read indoors
Mapping apps only work over Wi-Fi
The phone's compass is broken
explanation: Satellite positioning depends on receiving weak signals from several satellites at once, and roofs and floors block them. Indoors the phone estimates location from known Wi-Fi access points and cell towers, which is accurate to tens or hundreds of metres rather than a few metres, hence the jumping. This is normal behaviour, not a fault. The SIM is unaffected by buildings, mapping works over any data connection, and the compass gives heading rather than position.

distractor_analysis.1: SIM operation does not depend on the phone's surroundings.
distractor_analysis.2: Maps work over cellular data as well as Wi-Fi.
distractor_analysis.3: A compass fault would affect the direction arrow, not the position.

question: Which technology allows a phone to determine its position using signals from orbiting satellites?
options: GPS and other global navigation satellite systems
NFC
Bluetooth
Cellular triangulation
explanation: Phones include a receiver for GPS and usually for other constellations such as Galileo, GLONASS and BeiDou, which are collectively called global navigation satellite systems. The receiver measures the time of arrival of signals from at least four satellites to compute a position, typically within a few metres outdoors. The receiver is passive and works without a data plan, although maps need data to download. Cellular triangulation is a fallback estimate, and NFC and Bluetooth are short-range links.

distractor_analysis.1: NFC operates over centimetres and has no positioning role.
distractor_analysis.2: Bluetooth beacons can assist indoors but do not provide global positioning.
distractor_analysis.3: Cell triangulation is a coarse fallback, not the satellite technology asked about.

question: A company issues phones and wants to enforce a passcode, push corporate Wi-Fi settings and remotely wipe a lost device. Which type of system provides these controls?
options: Mobile device management (MDM)
A mobile hotspot
A cloud photo backup service
A Bluetooth beacon network
explanation: MDM platforms enrol phones and tablets so an administrator can push configuration profiles, require a passcode and encryption, install or block apps, and wipe or lock a device that is lost. Devices are enrolled either automatically through the vendor's business programme or manually with an enrolment app or profile. MDM is the foundation of corporate mobile support. Hotspots, photo backup and beacons solve entirely different problems.

distractor_analysis.1: A hotspot shares a data connection.
distractor_analysis.2: Photo backup protects pictures, not device policy.
distractor_analysis.3: Beacons provide indoor location, not management.

question: An employee wants to use a personal phone for work email. The company requires that corporate data can be removed without touching personal photos and messages. Which MDM approach satisfies this?
options: A bring-your-own-device policy using a managed work profile or container with selective wipe
Full device enrolment with mandatory factory reset on departure
Disabling the phone's camera
Requiring the phone to stay on the office Wi-Fi
explanation: Modern MDM separates work and personal data on a personal device. Android creates a work profile and iOS uses managed apps and accounts, so corporate email, contacts and files live in a container that the administrator controls. When the employee leaves, a selective wipe removes only that container and leaves personal content untouched. A full factory reset would violate the requirement, and camera or network restrictions do not address data separation.

distractor_analysis.1: A factory reset destroys the employee's personal data.
distractor_analysis.2: Disabling the camera is a policy control unrelated to data separation.
distractor_analysis.3: Network restrictions do not partition data on the device.

question: A sales team's phones must sign in to corporate email with a certificate instead of a password, and the certificate must be installed on every phone without user involvement. Which mechanism does this?
options: A configuration profile pushed by the MDM containing the account settings and certificate
Emailing each user a PDF with instructions
Enabling Bluetooth file sharing
Setting the phones to airplane mode during setup
explanation: MDM configuration profiles are signed bundles of settings: mail accounts, Wi-Fi networks, VPN definitions, certificates and restrictions. When pushed to an enrolled phone, the settings apply silently, so every device gets the same account and certificate with no user typing. This is how enterprises deploy certificate-based authentication at scale. Manual instructions do not scale and invite errors, Bluetooth sharing is insecure for credentials, and airplane mode blocks the push.

distractor_analysis.1: Manual steps on hundreds of phones are slow and error-prone.
distractor_analysis.2: Bluetooth sharing is not a management channel.
distractor_analysis.3: Airplane mode disconnects the phone from the MDM server.

question: A user configures a corporate email account on a phone using only an email address and password, and the phone finds the server settings automatically. Which feature made this possible?
options: Autodiscover, which looks up the mail server configuration from the domain
Bluetooth pairing with the mail server
A hotspot connection
GPS location services
explanation: Modern mail systems such as Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace publish their server details so a client can look them up from the domain part of the address. The phone queries the autodiscover record, retrieves the server names, ports and security settings, and completes the account with just the credentials. If autodiscover is missing the user must enter incoming and outgoing server settings manually, which is where support calls come from.

distractor_analysis.1: Bluetooth has no role in email configuration.
distractor_analysis.2: A hotspot provides connectivity but not server settings.
distractor_analysis.3: Location services do not discover mail servers.

question: A user sets up a personal email account on a phone and finds that deleting a message on the phone does not remove it from the webmail inbox. Which protocol is the phone most likely using?
options: POP3, which downloads messages and does not keep the mailbox in sync
IMAP, which keeps every client synchronised with the server
Exchange ActiveSync
SMTP
explanation: POP3 pulls copies of messages to the device and, depending on settings, leaves the originals on the server, so actions on one device are not reflected anywhere else. IMAP and Exchange ActiveSync keep the mailbox on the server and synchronise every folder and read or delete state to all clients, which is the behaviour users expect today. Switching the account to IMAP fixes the complaint. SMTP only sends mail and never affects the inbox.

distractor_analysis.1: IMAP would have deleted the message everywhere.
distractor_analysis.2: ActiveSync synchronises state across devices in the same way as IMAP.
distractor_analysis.3: SMTP is the outgoing protocol and does not manage the inbox.

question: A user must manually configure a mail account on a phone. The provider says incoming mail uses IMAP over SSL and outgoing uses SMTP with STARTTLS. Which port pair is correct?
options: Incoming 993, outgoing 587
Incoming 110, outgoing 25
Incoming 143, outgoing 465
Incoming 995, outgoing 80
explanation: IMAP over an implicit SSL/TLS connection listens on TCP 993, and the modern client submission port for SMTP, which starts unencrypted and upgrades with STARTTLS, is TCP 587. Port 110 is plain POP3 and 25 is server-to-server relay that most providers block for clients. Port 143 is unencrypted IMAP, 465 is SMTP over implicit TLS rather than STARTTLS, and 995 is POP3 over SSL with 80 being HTTP. Matching the port to the encryption method is what makes the account connect.

distractor_analysis.1: 110 and 25 are unencrypted POP3 and relay SMTP.
distractor_analysis.2: 143 is IMAP without encryption and 465 is implicit TLS rather than STARTTLS.
distractor_analysis.3: 995 is secure POP3 and 80 is web traffic.

question: A user replaced a lost phone and, after signing in to the same account, found contacts, calendar and photos restored automatically. Which feature made this happen?
options: Cloud synchronisation and backup tied to the user's account
Bluetooth transfer from the old phone
A SIM card swap
An MDM remote wipe
explanation: Both major platforms continuously synchronise contacts, calendars, notes and settings to the account in the cloud, and take periodic full backups over Wi-Fi. Signing in on a new device pulls that data back down. Technicians should confirm backup is enabled and has run recently before any repair or replacement. The old phone was lost, so no local transfer was possible; a SIM only carries the subscriber identity, and a wipe removes data rather than restoring it.

distractor_analysis.1: The old phone was lost, so it could not be the source.
distractor_analysis.2: A SIM does not store contacts or photos in modern use.
distractor_analysis.3: A remote wipe erases a device.

question: A user complains that photos taken on the phone do not appear on the laptop even though both use the same cloud account. The phone has been on cellular data all day. What is the most likely reason?
options: Photo synchronisation is set to upload over Wi-Fi only and the phone has not been on Wi-Fi
The laptop needs a SIM card
The photos are too high resolution to sync
Bluetooth is disabled on the laptop
explanation: Cloud photo services default to uploading over Wi-Fi to protect the user's cellular allowance, so pictures taken away from Wi-Fi queue up until the phone returns to a wireless network. The user can either join Wi-Fi or enable cellular upload in the app settings. Laptops do not need SIMs to reach cloud services, resolution does not block sync, and Bluetooth plays no part in cloud synchronisation.

distractor_analysis.1: The laptop reaches the cloud over its own internet connection.
distractor_analysis.2: Cloud services accept full-resolution photos.
distractor_analysis.3: Cloud sync runs over the internet, not Bluetooth.

question: A phone's storage is full and the user is told that enabling cloud photo storage will help. How does that feature typically free space?
options: Full-resolution originals are kept in the cloud and the phone keeps smaller optimised versions
Photos are compressed to black and white
Photos are moved to the SIM card
The phone deletes all photos older than a week
explanation: Optimised storage keeps the original files safely in the account and replaces local copies with device-sized versions, downloading the original on demand when the user opens or edits a picture. This can free many gigabytes without losing anything. Users should understand that the originals now depend on the account and that a full-resolution download needs connectivity. Colour is unchanged, SIMs hold no photos, and nothing is deleted from the account.

distractor_analysis.1: Optimised versions are full colour, just smaller.
distractor_analysis.2: SIM cards hold kilobytes of subscriber data, not photos.
distractor_analysis.3: Photos remain in the cloud indefinitely.

question: An administrator needs to locate a company tablet that was left in a taxi and then erase it if it cannot be recovered. Which capability of the management platform does this rely on?
options: Remote locate and remote wipe on an enrolled device
Bluetooth tethering
Configuration profile for Wi-Fi
App store restrictions
explanation: MDM and the platform vendors' own services can report an enrolled device's last known location, play a sound, lock it with a message, and finally wipe it. The wipe command executes as soon as the device next connects to any network, which is why the device should be locked first rather than wiped immediately if there is a chance of recovery. Tethering, Wi-Fi profiles and app restrictions are unrelated to finding or erasing a lost device.

distractor_analysis.1: Tethering shares data; it does not locate anything.
distractor_analysis.2: A Wi-Fi profile configures networks, not device recovery.
distractor_analysis.3: App restrictions control what can be installed.

question: A company wants every corporate phone to require two-factor authentication for its email app and to block the app from copying text into personal apps. Which category of MDM control handles the copy restriction?
options: Mobile application management (MAM) or app protection policies
Wi-Fi configuration profiles
Remote wipe
Location services
explanation: Application-level management applies policy inside managed apps: requiring a PIN or biometric to open the app, blocking cut and paste to unmanaged apps, preventing saving to personal storage and encrypting app data. It works alongside device enrolment and is the only way to enforce these controls on a personal device. Wi-Fi profiles, remote wipe and location are device-level features that do not govern data movement between apps.

distractor_analysis.1: Wi-Fi profiles push network settings.
distractor_analysis.2: Remote wipe erases; it does not govern day-to-day data flow.
distractor_analysis.3: Location services report position and do not control clipboard use.

question: A user cannot enrol a new phone in the company's MDM. The enrolment app reports that the device is not eligible. The phone was bought second-hand. What is the most likely cause?
options: The device is still registered to the previous owner's account or management, an activation lock
The phone's Bluetooth is off
The phone has too much free storage
The user has not set a wallpaper
explanation: Both platforms tie a device to the account or organisation that last activated it. A second-hand phone whose previous owner did not sign out and remove it stays locked to that owner, and a phone previously enrolled by another company stays in that company's management programme. Enrolment is refused until the previous party releases it. This is also why corporate procurement prefers devices bought through channels that register them directly to the company.

distractor_analysis.1: Enrolment works over Wi-Fi or cellular and does not need Bluetooth.
distractor_analysis.2: Free storage is never a barrier to enrolment.
distractor_analysis.3: Wallpaper is cosmetic.

question: A user asks what the tiny removable card in the phone's side tray is for. What is the correct answer?
options: It is the SIM, which identifies the subscriber to the carrier's network
It stores all the user's photos
It holds the phone's operating system
It is the Bluetooth antenna
explanation: The subscriber identity module carries the account identity and authentication key that let the carrier recognise the phone on its network. Moving the SIM to another unlocked phone moves the number and plan with it. Many current phones also or only support an eSIM, a built-in chip provisioned electronically by the carrier, which is why some models have no tray. Photos and the operating system live in the phone's own flash storage, and the antennas are internal to the chassis.

distractor_analysis.1: Photos are stored in the phone's internal storage or the cloud.
distractor_analysis.2: The operating system is on internal flash, not a removable card.
distractor_analysis.3: Antennas are built into the frame or display assembly.

question: A traveller wants to use a local carrier's data plan abroad without removing the home SIM. The phone supports eSIM. What should the technician recommend?
options: Add the local carrier's eSIM profile alongside the physical SIM and select it for data
Cut the home SIM down to fit a second tray
Enable Bluetooth tethering to a local phone
Use airplane mode for the whole trip
explanation: An eSIM is a programmable chip in the phone that stores one or more carrier profiles. A traveller can buy a local or travel data plan online, scan a QR code to add the profile, and set that line for data while keeping the home number active for calls and texts. This avoids roaming charges and the risk of losing a tiny plastic card. Cutting SIMs risks damage, tethering depends on someone else's phone, and airplane mode disconnects everything.

distractor_analysis.1: Cutting a SIM can destroy it and most phones have one tray.
distractor_analysis.2: Tethering to another person's phone is not a plan of one's own.
distractor_analysis.3: Airplane mode removes connectivity rather than adding a plan.

question: A phone shows full cellular bars but calls fail and data is very slow in a packed stadium. What is the most likely cause?
options: The local cell is congested by the number of users, so capacity rather than signal is the limit
The SIM has expired
The phone's antenna is damaged
Airplane mode is on
explanation: Signal bars measure how strongly the phone hears the tower, not how much capacity the tower has left. In a crowd tens of thousands of phones share one cell, and the radio channels and backhaul saturate, so calls fail to set up and data crawls despite excellent signal. Carriers add temporary cells at big events for this reason. An expired SIM shows no service everywhere, a damaged antenna shows weak bars, and airplane mode shows no bars at all.

distractor_analysis.1: An expired SIM fails everywhere, not only in the stadium.
distractor_analysis.2: Antenna damage reduces signal strength rather than leaving full bars.
distractor_analysis.3: Airplane mode removes the signal indicator entirely.

question: A user in a building with poor cellular coverage still receives calls on the phone over the office Wi-Fi. Which feature is in use?
options: Wi-Fi calling
Bluetooth calling
NFC calling
Satellite calling
explanation: Wi-Fi calling routes voice calls and texts over any internet connection to the carrier's core network, so the phone behaves as though it has cellular coverage even in a basement or a rural house. It must be enabled in the phone settings and supported by the carrier, and an emergency address is registered so emergency services can locate the caller. Bluetooth carries audio to a headset but not calls to the network, NFC is for taps, and satellite messaging on some phones is emergency text only.

distractor_analysis.1: Bluetooth links the phone to accessories, not to the carrier.
distractor_analysis.2: NFC cannot carry a voice call.
distractor_analysis.3: Satellite features are for emergency messaging, not everyday calls.

question: A phone's battery drains far faster than usual after the user moved to an office at the edge of cellular coverage. Which explanation is most likely?
options: The cellular radio is transmitting at maximum power to hold a weak signal
The phone's storage is nearly full
The screen protector is too thick
The user's contacts list is too long
explanation: A phone continuously adjusts its transmit power to reach the tower. At the edge of coverage it runs the radio near full power and repeatedly searches for a better cell, and that is one of the biggest battery drains on any handset. Enabling Wi-Fi calling, so the phone can prefer the office Wi-Fi for voice and data, usually restores normal battery life. Storage, protectors and contacts have no effect on power consumption.

distractor_analysis.1: Full storage slows the phone but does not drain the battery.
distractor_analysis.2: A protector is passive glass or film.
distractor_analysis.3: Contact list size is trivial data with no power cost.

question: A company wants to allow only approved apps on its warehouse scanners and prevent staff from opening anything else. Which MDM feature provides this?
options: Kiosk or single-app mode with an allow list of applications
Remote wipe
Wi-Fi calling
Cloud photo backup
explanation: Dedicated-device or kiosk mode locks a handset to one app or a small allow list, hides the home screen and settings, and can prevent the device leaving the app even after a reboot. It is the standard configuration for scanners, point-of-sale tablets and public displays. Remote wipe is for lost devices, Wi-Fi calling is a voice feature, and photo backup is a consumer service; none of them restricts which apps run.

distractor_analysis.1: Remote wipe erases a device and does not control app use.
distractor_analysis.2: Wi-Fi calling is about voice over wireless networks.
distractor_analysis.3: Photo backup does not restrict applications.

question: After enrolling in MDM, a user's phone shows a corporate Wi-Fi network as connected but a corporate intranet site is unreachable while public sites load. Which is the most likely cause?
options: The VPN profile pushed by the MDM has not connected or was not included, so internal resources are unreachable
The phone's SIM card is missing
The screen brightness is too low
The phone's storage is full
explanation: Internal sites normally sit behind the corporate firewall and require a VPN or a per-app VPN tunnel that the MDM configures. If the VPN profile is missing, the certificate has not arrived, or the user has not authenticated to it, public internet works but intranet names fail. Checking the VPN status in settings and confirming the profile installed is the fix. SIM, brightness and storage have no bearing on reaching internal sites.

distractor_analysis.1: The phone is on Wi-Fi; cellular identity is irrelevant.
distractor_analysis.2: Brightness is a display setting.
distractor_analysis.3: Full storage does not block network destinations.

question: A user's phone contacts are duplicated after adding a second account. What is the recommended first step?
options: Check which accounts are set to sync contacts and disable contact sync on the redundant account
Factory reset the phone
Remove the SIM card
Turn off Wi-Fi
explanation: Each account on a phone can sync its own contacts, calendar and mail. When two accounts hold copies of the same people, the phone shows both sets. Turning off contact sync for one account, or using the contacts app's merge duplicates feature, cleans the list without losing data. A factory reset is far out of proportion, the SIM rarely stores contacts on modern phones, and Wi-Fi has nothing to do with which accounts sync.

distractor_analysis.1: A reset wipes the device for a settings problem.
distractor_analysis.2: Modern contacts live in accounts, not on the SIM.
distractor_analysis.3: Wi-Fi state does not change account sync settings.

question: Before sending a phone for a screen repair, what should a technician ask the user to do to protect their data?
options: Confirm a current cloud or computer backup exists, then sign out of accounts or enable a passcode as policy requires
Remove the screen protector
Turn off Bluetooth
Delete all photos to save space
explanation: A repair can end in a replaced or wiped device, so the essential protection is a verified backup taken to the cloud or a computer immediately beforehand. Many repair shops also require the activation lock to be disabled, which means signing out of the platform account, and corporate policy may instead require the passcode to stay on. Protectors and Bluetooth are irrelevant, and deleting photos destroys exactly what the backup is meant to preserve.

distractor_analysis.1: The protector has no bearing on data safety.
distractor_analysis.2: Bluetooth state does not protect data.
distractor_analysis.3: Deleting photos is data loss, not protection.

question: A user complains that a phone connects to a public Wi-Fi hotspot at a cafe automatically every visit, which the company security team has told staff to avoid. What setting resolves this?
options: Forget the network or disable auto-join for that network
Enable airplane mode permanently
Remove the SIM card
Increase the screen timeout
explanation: Phones remember networks they have joined and rejoin them automatically. Forgetting the network removes the saved profile, and most phones also offer a per-network auto-join toggle so the network can be used deliberately but not automatically. MDM can go further and block unmanaged networks. Airplane mode would remove all connectivity, the SIM is unrelated to Wi-Fi, and screen timeout is a display setting.

distractor_analysis.1: Airplane mode disables cellular too, which is not wanted.
distractor_analysis.2: Wi-Fi does not depend on the SIM.
distractor_analysis.3: Screen timeout affects the display only.

question: A corporate phone's email stopped syncing after the user changed their domain password on a laptop. Other apps work. What is the most likely fix?
options: Update the stored password for the mail account on the phone
Replace the SIM
Reset network settings
Turn off location services
explanation: Mail clients store the account credential and present it on every sync. When the password changes elsewhere, the phone keeps offering the old one, the server rejects it and sync stops, sometimes silently or with a re-enter password prompt. Entering the new password in the account settings restores sync; repeated failures can also lock the account, so acting quickly matters. Network reset, SIM and location services are unrelated to a credential mismatch.

distractor_analysis.1: The SIM has nothing to do with email authentication.
distractor_analysis.2: Network settings are fine because other apps work.
distractor_analysis.3: Location services do not affect mail sync.

question: A user has Bluetooth enabled and a Wi-Fi hotspot running on the phone at the same time and notices the hotspot is slow. Both radios share the same band. Which band is that?
options: 2.4 GHz
5 GHz
6 GHz
900 MHz
explanation: Bluetooth operates in the 2.4 GHz band, the same band used by 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, so a phone acting as a hotspot on 2.4 GHz while streaming to Bluetooth earbuds is competing with itself, and microwave ovens and neighbours' networks add more interference. Switching the hotspot to 5 GHz, where the phone supports it, moves the Wi-Fi traffic out of the crowded band. 6 GHz is Wi-Fi 6E and 7 only, and 900 MHz is used by cellular and some IoT radios, not Bluetooth.

distractor_analysis.1: Bluetooth does not use 5 GHz.
distractor_analysis.2: 6 GHz is reserved for newer Wi-Fi standards.
distractor_analysis.3: 900 MHz is a cellular and IoT band, not Bluetooth.

question: A phone is enrolled in MDM and the administrator has enforced a six-digit passcode and encryption. The user asks why encryption matters if there is already a passcode. What is the accurate answer?
options: Encryption protects the stored data if the storage is read directly, while the passcode only guards the normal user interface
Encryption makes the phone charge faster
Encryption is required for Bluetooth to work
Encryption removes the need for backups
explanation: A passcode stops someone using the phone through its screen, but without encryption the flash storage could be read with forensic tools. Device encryption scrambles the storage with a key derived in part from the passcode and stored in secure hardware, so the data is unreadable without both. Modern phones encrypt by default, and MDM enforces it so the setting cannot be turned off. Encryption has no effect on charging or Bluetooth and does not replace backups.

distractor_analysis.1: Encryption is a security control with no effect on charging.
distractor_analysis.2: Bluetooth operates independently of storage encryption.
distractor_analysis.3: Encrypted data can still be lost; backups remain essential.

question: A small business owner asks whether staff phones need MDM if they only use web email. Which benefit of MDM is still relevant?
options: Enforcing screen lock and encryption and being able to wipe a lost phone that holds cached company data
Making the phones charge faster
Providing GPS satellites
Increasing cellular signal strength
explanation: Even a browser caches credentials, cookies and downloaded attachments, and staff inevitably store contacts and messages. MDM ensures every phone has a lock screen and encryption and gives the business a way to wipe a device that goes missing, which is the minimum most data protection rules expect. The other options are not things any management platform can do; charging, satellites and radio signal are physical matters.

distractor_analysis.1: Charging speed is hardware and charger dependent.
distractor_analysis.2: GPS satellites are operated by governments, not MDM vendors.
distractor_analysis.3: Signal strength depends on the carrier network.

question: A user's phone shows a Wi-Fi symbol with an exclamation mark and apps report no connection, but the laptop on the same network is fine. Which step is most likely to resolve it?
options: Forget and rejoin the Wi-Fi network, or toggle Wi-Fi off and on, to obtain a fresh network address
Replace the phone's battery
Remove the screen protector
Change the ringtone
explanation: The exclamation indicator means the phone is associated but has no working route to the internet, commonly because its DHCP lease failed or a stale address is in use. Rejoining the network forces a new address and DNS settings from the router. If every device were affected the router would be the suspect, but a working laptop points at the phone's own connection state. Battery, protector and ringtone have nothing to do with networking.

distractor_analysis.1: Battery condition does not affect IP addressing.
distractor_analysis.2: A protector is passive.
distractor_analysis.3: Ringtones are unrelated to connectivity.

question: A technician is asked to explain the difference between synchronising a phone to the cloud and backing it up. Which statement is accurate?
options: Sync keeps live data such as contacts identical across devices, while a backup is a point-in-time copy used to restore a device
Sync and backup are the same operation
Backups only include photos
Sync only works over a cable
explanation: Synchronisation continuously mirrors changing data, so deleting a contact on one device deletes it everywhere, which means sync alone cannot recover from a mistake. A backup captures the whole device at a moment, including app data and settings, and is what a replacement phone is restored from. Both are needed. Backups include far more than photos, and both sync and backup normally run over Wi-Fi.

distractor_analysis.1: They serve different purposes and behave differently on deletion.
distractor_analysis.2: Backups cover settings, app data, messages and more.
distractor_analysis.3: Sync is wireless by default.

question: A company is deciding between issuing corporate phones and allowing personal phones for work. Which TWO statements about MDM are accurate? (Select TWO.)
options: Corporate-owned devices can be fully managed, including complete wipe and strict restrictions
Personal devices are typically managed with a work profile or managed apps so only corporate data is controlled
MDM can only manage devices from one manufacturer
MDM requires every phone to be connected by USB to the administrator's computer
MDM cannot enforce a passcode
explanation: Ownership determines the management model. A company-owned device can be supervised or fully managed, with every setting under administrative control and a full wipe available. A personal device is enrolled with a work profile or managed apps so the company controls only its own data and can remove just that. MDM platforms manage iOS, Android and often Windows and macOS together, they work entirely over the network, and enforcing passcodes is one of their basic functions.

distractor_analysis.2: Major MDM platforms manage several vendors' devices.
distractor_analysis.3: Enrolment and policy are delivered over the air.
distractor_analysis.4: Passcode enforcement is a core MDM capability.

question: A user is about to travel internationally with a corporate phone. Which TWO actions should the technician recommend before departure? (Select TWO.)
options: Confirm the plan includes roaming or add a travel plan or local eSIM
Verify that a current backup has completed
Remove the passcode so border staff can use the phone
Disable encryption to improve battery life abroad
Delete the MDM enrolment to avoid foreign network conflicts
explanation: Travel preparation is about cost and recovery. Sorting out roaming or a local data plan avoids bill shock, and a fresh backup means a lost or damaged phone can be replaced abroad with minimal disruption. Security controls stay in place: the passcode and encryption protect the device if it is lost, and MDM enrolment is what allows the company to locate and wipe it, so none of those should be removed.

distractor_analysis.2: Removing the passcode leaves company data exposed if the phone is lost.
distractor_analysis.3: Encryption has no meaningful battery cost and protects the data.
distractor_analysis.4: Enrolment is what enables remote help and wipe while travelling.

question: Match each mobile network or management term to its description.

pairs.right: Shares the phone's cellular data as a Wi-Fi network
Turns off all wireless radios with one switch
Carrier profile stored on a chip inside the phone
Central platform that enforces policy on enrolled devices
Routes voice calls through an internet connection

explanation: These terms come up constantly in mobile support. A hotspot shares connectivity outward, airplane mode is the master radio switch, an eSIM replaces the plastic card with a programmable profile, MDM is how organisations control fleets of phones, and Wi-Fi calling rescues voice service where the cellular signal is poor. Being able to name the right feature for a user's situation is most of the job.

question: Order the steps an administrator should take when an enrolled corporate phone is reported lost.
sequence: Confirm the report and identify the device record in the management console
Use remote locate to see the last known position and try to contact the finder if appropriate
Lock the device remotely with a message and contact number displayed on the screen
If the device is not recovered within the agreed time, issue a remote wipe
Record the incident, retire the device record and provision a replacement from backup
explanation: The order protects data without destroying recovery chances. Verifying the report avoids wiping a phone that is in a desk drawer. Locating and locking come before wiping because a locked, encrypted phone is already safe from casual access and may still be returned. A wipe is the final step because it is irreversible. Closing the record and restoring the user from backup completes the process and keeps the asset register accurate.

question: A user says the phone's mobile data works but only very slowly on the last day of every month, then recovers. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The plan's high-speed data allowance is used up and the carrier throttles speed until the cycle resets
The SIM card wears out toward the end of the month
The phone's battery is weaker at month end
Cellular towers shut down for maintenance monthly
explanation: Most plans include a monthly allowance of full-speed data. Once it is consumed the carrier reduces the connection to a low speed rather than cutting it off, and the pattern of slowness that resets on the billing date is the tell-tale sign. The fix is a larger plan, using Wi-Fi more, or checking which apps consume the most data in the phone's usage screen. SIMs do not wear, battery state does not throttle data, and towers do not have a monthly outage.

distractor_analysis.1: A SIM is a passive chip with no monthly cycle.
distractor_analysis.2: Battery level does not affect data speed.
distractor_analysis.3: Carriers do not take networks down on a monthly schedule.
